chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan (may God be pleased with him) narrated that Ahmad ibn Idris narrated from Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya ibn Imran al-Ash'ari, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and others, linking it up through their chain to As-Sadiq (peace be upon him) who said:

Shame (al-haya') consists of ten parts: nine are in women and one in men. When the girl begins menstruation, one part of her shame is lost; when she marries, one part is lost; when she has sexual intercourse (iftira'), one part is lost; when she gives birth, one part is lost, leaving one part, so five parts remain for her. If she commits fornication, all her shame is lost; and if she remains chaste, the five parts remain for her.

key_terms.الِافْتِرَاعُ: Sexual intercourse, specifically in the context of marriage
key_terms.الْجَارِيَةُ: The girl, referring to a young female before marriage
key_terms.الْحَيَاءُ: Modesty or shame, a key ethical virtue

ai.seo_question: How does a woman's share of modesty change according to life events in Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) outlines a nuanced view of modesty (hayā') as a dynamic quality that diminishes with specific biological and social transitions—menstruation, marriage, intercourse, and childbirth—leaving women with five parts. This reduction is not a loss of virtue but a natural progression, preserved fully if the woman maintains chastity, whereas fornication results in the complete loss of this spiritual attribute. This hadith highlights the Shia emphasis on the interplay between natural human development and moral integrity in preserving dignity.
